title: Incredible 2,000-Year-Old Roman Shipwreck Found Off Sicily, Loaded with Amphorae
summary: When Sicilian fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola spotted an unusual shape on his seabed scanner, he assumed it was a large rock. Instead, he found himself face-to-face with a 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck — an encounter he described as the most incredible discovery of his life. The wreck, located about 150 feet deep near Mazara del Vallo, measures 69 feet long and 20 feet wide. It is piled high with hundreds of well-preserved amphorae, the tall ceramic jars that ancient Romans used to transport wine, olive oil, and grain across the Mediterranean. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," De Mola wrote on social media. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again." His video of the site shows eels, snappers, and countless marine creatures weaving through the jars, transforming the wreck into an accidental artificial reef. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the find as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years." Experts date the vessel to the 2nd or 1st century BC. Specialist divers from the Carabinieri Art Squad, a police unit dedicated to cultural heritage protection, have secured the site while archaeologists work to determine the ship's origin and the nature of its cargo. The Mediterranean seabed is littered with similar wrecks — another 1st or 2nd century BC vessel was found northwest of Rome in 2023 — but each discovery offers a rare, tangible link to the ancient maritime trade networks that shaped the classical world. For De Mola, the experience was humbling: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."
why_it_matters: Discoveries like this show that history isn’t just in textbooks—it lies hidden beneath the sea, waiting for ordinary people to find it. For a teenager, the story highlights how curiosity, local knowledge, and respect for cultural heritage can connect you directly to the ancient world and inspire careers in marine archaeology or conservation.

background_read: The Mediterranean Sea was the highway of the Roman Empire, and ancient ships routinely carried cargoes of wine, olive oil, fish sauce (garum), and grain in amphorae. Sicily, positioned at a crossroads, was a vital trading hub; the port of Mazara del Vallo has been active since at least the Phoenician period.

Roman shipwrecks like this one often survive remarkably well because wooden hulls become buried in sediment and are protected from oxygen. Previous famous finds, such as the Antikythera wreck (which held an ancient geared “computer”) and the underwater archaeological park of Baiae near Naples, have shown how much of Rome’s daily life sits on the seafloor.

Italy’s Carabinieri Art Squad (formally the Comando Carabinieri per la Tutela del Patrimonio Culturale) is the world’s oldest police unit dedicated to art and archaeology. Founded in 1969, it recovers stolen artifacts and guards cultural sites on land and underwater.

This discovery is part of a pattern: in 2023, another 2,000‑year‑old wreck was found northwest of Rome, and in recent years fishermen have spotted several wrecks off Spain and Greece. Technology like side‑scan sonar and affordable underwater drones have made it easier for amateurs and professionals to find such missing pieces of history.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists and locals celebrate the find as a window into Roman trade and daily life. Intact amphorae can reveal details about ancient diets, economy, and even the ship’s route, adding to our understanding of a vast maritime network that connected three continents.

Once known, shipwrecks become vulnerable to treasure hunters and even well‑meaning souvenir collectors. Disturbing a site without proper scientific methods destroys irreplaceable context, which is why rapid protection by units like the Carabinieri Art Squad is essential.

While the archaeological treasure is the main focus, the wreck also functions as an artificial reef, boosting local marine biodiversity. This dual identity creates tension: opening the site for study or tourism could damage the new ecosystem, requiring careful planning.

As seabed scanners and underwater drones become cheaper, more wrecks will be found by citizens. This raises the need for updated international laws on underwater cultural heritage and cooperation between governments, scientists, and local communities to decide what to excavate, preserve, or leave as underwater museums.
